extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and practitioners of art and architecture interested in identifying and judging Gothic buildings
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules and qualitative criteria for determining whether a building is Gothic and whether it is good architecture, with guidance on ornament, masonry, sculpture, and proportion (Ruskin's tests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Steep gabled roof
rubrics_metrics.description: "Look if the roof rises in a steep gable, high above the walls."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the roof does not rise in a steep gable, there is something wrong; the building is not quite pure Gothic, or has been altered. Presence of the steep gable is a primary indicator of Gothic purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointed arches with gables over principal openings
rubrics_metrics.description: "Look if the principal windows and doors have pointed arches with gables over them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not pointed arches, the building is not Gothic; if they have not any gables over them, it is either not pure, or not first-rate. If a building has steep roof, pointed arch, and gable united, it is nearly certain to be a Gothic building of a very fine time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cusped arches or foliated apertures (foliation present)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Look if the arches are cusped, or apertures foliated."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the building meets the first two conditions it is sure to be foliated somewhere; if not everywhere, unfoliated parts are imperfect unless they are large bearing arches or small and sharp grouped arches forming foliation by multiplicity. If there is no foliation anywhere, the building is assuredly imperfect Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arches carried on true shafts with bases and capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: "Look if its arches in general... are carried on true shafts with bases and capitals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If present, the building is assuredly of the finest Gothic style (though it may still be an imitation). Exceptions: if apertures have plain, unmoulded sides, the building may still be fine (domestic or military adaptation). But if sides are moulded and yet there are no capitals at the spring of the arch, it is assuredly of an inferior school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent vigour of workmanship ('built by strong men')
rubrics_metrics.description: "See if it looks as if it had been built by strong men; if it has the sort of roughness, and largeness, and nonchalance, mixed... with exquisite tenderness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buildings that display roughness, largeness, and nonchalance (a broad vision and massy power) are usually noble. Overly accurate, minute, and scrupulous workmanship is suspicious—either the very best or the very worst; commonly a sign of the worst (mechanism replacing design). Very accurate workmanship without other merits may be passed with contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregularity of parts (functional, not slavish symmetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Observe if it be irregular, its different parts fitting themselves to different purposes..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one part always answers accurately to another part, it is sure to be a bad building. Greater and more conspicuous irregularities increase the chances that the building is a good one (example: deliberate non-central placement in the Ducal Palace indicates mastery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual variation in traceries and ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: "Observe if all the traceries, capitals, and other ornaments are of perpetually varied design."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If they are not of perpetually varied design, the work is assuredly bad. Repetition of the same idea (unchanging foliation) is a defect of later Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture must be legible and properly scaled
rubrics_metrics.description: "Read the sculpture... the sculpture is always so set, and on such a scale, that at the ordinary distance from which the edifice is seen, the sculpture shall be thoroughly intelligible and interesting."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legibility: uppermost statues will be ten or twelve feet high, upper ornamentation colossal, increasing in fineness as it descends, so that details near the foundation can be as fine as cabinet-work. After confirming legibility, sculpture should be 'read' and judged like a book; its intelligibility at normal viewing distance is essential to value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition integrity (nothing removable without harm)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A composition from which anything can be removed without doing mischief is always so far forth inferior."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work of art (or architecture) should be such that removing any significant element diminishes it; if parts can be removed without harm, the composition is of inferior quality. This is a fundamental test of artistic completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface‑Gothic vs Linear‑Gothic distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition and contrast: Surface-Gothic (Veronese) depends on broad sculptured surfaces, strong masonry, simple masses, perpetual variety; Linear-Gothic (late French/English Perpendicular) depends on multiplications of similar lines of tracery, intricate lines, weak masonry, broken mass, and repeated ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin argues the Italian/Surface-Gothic is the nobler style because it is strong in masonry, simple in masses, and perpetual in variety; the Late/Linear schools, though graceful, are weaker and more repetitive. Compare whether ornamentation emphasizes broad sculptured surfaces or lace-like tracery; preference is for the former for longevity and nobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence of figure sculpture (not shrouded by tracery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Gothic: figure sculpture is vigorous, prominent, and essential; Late Gothic: sculpture is often enfeebled and shrouded in tracery and may be removable with little harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether figure sculpture is an integral, readable element of the façade or merely ornament hidden by tracery. Sculpture that can be removed without harming the effect indicates a degraded approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization of ornament as a sign of earlier date
rubrics_metrics.description: The Byzantine and early Gothic tendency to centralize ornament (central capital or midmost carved piece made superior) vs later buildings where capitals are all different or ungrouped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When capitals in a grouped set are centralized (central one distinct, the lateral ones answering each other), it often indicates an earlier building. Loss of such centralization (all capitals different or ungrouped) is a sign of relative lateness (e.g., Ducal Palace did away with subtle centralization). This is useful for dating and assessing stylistic development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracery adapted logically to structure (masonry/joint placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper structural adaptation of traceries: e.g., in Ducal Palace the quatrefoil was placed between arches (not above) so bearing power is thrown between quatrefoils; joints placed centrally in quatrefoils and additional right-angled joints to manage load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether traceries are merely decorative or are sensibly adapted to bear weight and serve structure. Correct placement of quatrefoils and masonry joints shows an architect's understanding of masonry and structural necessity rather than mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Palaces must be picturesque independently (intrinsic picturesqueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic palaces are 'picturesque in themselves' and would remain beautiful and strange even if sea, sky, and accessories were removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the building's form, massing, and ornament create intrinsic pictorial interest irrespective of setting. If its charm depends entirely on its surroundings, it is less characteristically Gothic (contrast with Renaissance palaces which owe much to contrast with their setting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincing appearance of lightness combined with structural strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic palaces show consummate strength joined with a lightness of form and sparingness of material; devices (string courses, chamfer filled with twisted shafts, twisted pillars at angles) are used to convince the eye of stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the building on whether visual devices successfully convey both lightness (economy of material) and assurance of stability. Elements such as twisted angle-shafts, chamfered corners with small shafts, bold string courses, and projected mouldings are indicators of deliberate means to achieve this balance.
